The firing of George Perlegos as chairman and chief executive of Atmel Corp. is an unusual case in that the man legally retaliated against those who coördinated the decision. Membership in the board of directors of Atmel Corp. used to be exclusively held by insiders, until a N.A.S.D.A.Q. rule requiring a majority of directors to be independent came into being. The five independent directors fired George & Gust Perlegos and two other executives on 7 Aug. 2006 in a board vote. George Perlegos claimed that a special shareholders' meeting was called before he was terminated; the result of the purported conference was that the five independent directors were themselves removed from office. Not surprisingly, the five independent directors disputed the allegation that such a convening occurred before George Perlegos was forced to quit. The five independent directors articulated the reasons behind George Perlegos's termination in a letter addressed to him as being "...based on your conduct in regard to personal and family air travel at company expense, and the lack of controls for preventing misuse of company resources." On 25 July 2001, the company launched an investigation into stock option grants' timings for the executives. What was not publicized was that a secret investigation to which only the independent directors were privy to was reviewed a few days before the announcement. This investigation concluded in Nov. 2005 that George Perlegos siphoned off $326K from corporate coffers in paying 338 air-line tickets for himself and his family. Gust Perlegos, who was the executive vice-president of Atmel Corp., was found separately to have misappropriated $80K in company funds to purchase 146 air-line tickets for his family and himself. Notably, the two investigations were not officially tied together by the company. The Perlegoses responded by filing three disparate suits in law against Atmel Corp. in Delaware state court, battles which were still raging at the time of publication of the cited New York Times article. The absence of a formal employment agreement meant the directors were within their rights to fire the Perlegoses, but George Perlegos countered that the travel cost violations were perpetrated by a terminated employee. Therefore, he argued that the independent directors went out of line in their fiduciarial capacities. A 27 Feb. 2009 W.S.J. article reveals the truth behind Mr. Dreier's so-called retirement as President, C.E.O., and Chairman of Ryland Group, Inc. on 29 May of the same year. Furthermore, Mr. Dreier earned a $900K salary for fiscal year 2009 along with both a to-be-determined bonus and $2 million cash in the same period. Moreover, the last three compensations mentioned were contingent upon Mr. Dreier's willingness to "treat his termination as a 'retirement'," as stated in a relevant S.E.C. filing. The article wrote, "A company spokesman said that Mr. Dreier's agreement to retire a year before his contract expires and before he is fully vested in all his retirement benefits will save the company money." There is more than meets the eye about Mr. Dreier's departure; the business was struggling in the aftermath of the national housing bubble burst and subsequent Great Recession. It is obvious that substantial material inducements in the form of what has been described above compelled Mr. Dreier to be terminated sooner than expected.

Cray Research Inc., once the gold standard for the very fastest computers in the world and the pride of the U.S. military, bowed to fiscal realities yesterday and said it would be acquired by computer workstation maker Silicon Graphics Inc. for about $740 million. The boards of both companies have approved the deal. According to the terms, Silicon Graphics will spend $585 million to buy 75 percent of the stock of Cray at $30 a share. In the following months, Silicon Graphics will swap its own shares for the remaining 25 percent of Cray stock. The companies expect to close the deal on April 1. News of the merger bolstered Cray's stock price yesterday by $3.62 1/2, to close at $28.87 1/2. Silicon Graphics investors were less upbeat, pushing that stock down $2.12 1/2 to end the day at $25.37 1/2. Gary Smaby, a longtime supercomputer analyst in Minneapolis, said the deal gives Silicon Graphics an entry to big institutions and corporate clients it lacked. And the price was right, he added. Cray's current value is only about 15 percent of its 1987 heyday value of about $4 billion -- about what Silicon Graphics is now worth, Smaby said.
